key: Ask what the method contains and where it acts. Estrogen means clotting risk and a scheduled withdrawal bleed; the depot injection means bone loss and slow return of fertility; the arm rod means unpredictable spotting; the levonorgestrel IUD acts locally and lightens periods; the copper IUD has no hormone, so periods get heavier.
items: Raises clotting factors and venous clot risk
chc
Ethinyl estradiol makes the liver produce more clotting factors, so estrogen-containing methods carry the venous clot risk that progestin-only and copper methods do not.
Avoided in smokers aged 35 or older and in migraine with aura
chc
Both conditions already raise stroke and clot risk, and estrogen adds to it, so these patients are steered to a progestin-only or nonhormonal method.
Hormone-free week gives a predictable withdrawal bleed
chc
Estrogen keeps the lining stable, and stopping the active hormones for a week lets it shed on schedule, so cycles are regular.
Taken as a daily pill, weekly patch or monthly vaginal ring
chc
All three formats deliver ethinyl estradiol with a progestin, so one set of estrogen contraindications covers the whole family.
Bone mineral density falls during use
dmpa
High, sustained medroxyprogesterone suppresses ovarian estradiol, and low estrogen speeds bone resorption, so density drops during use and partly recovers afterward.
Fertility can take many months to return after stopping
dmpa
The depot releases medroxyprogesterone slowly over months, so ovulation returns late, whereas fertility returns almost at once after the minipill or implant.
Injected every 3 months
dmpa
The depot keeps progestin levels high between injections, so a visit is needed about every 12 weeks instead of a daily action.
Rod placed under the skin of the upper arm
imp
The etonogestrel rod is inserted just beneath the skin and removed in a short office procedure, so it needs no daily action by the user.
Most effective reversible method
imp
Once the rod is in, nothing depends on the user and etonogestrel reliably blocks ovulation, so it has the lowest pregnancy rate of any reversible method.
Unpredictable spotting that may persist
imp
Etonogestrel suppresses ovulation strongly but does not stabilize the endometrium, so bleeding stays irregular.
Treats heavy menstrual bleeding by thinning the lining from inside the uterus
lng
Local levonorgestrel atrophies the endometrium, so menstrual blood loss falls sharply. This is why the device treats heavy periods as well as preventing pregnancy.
Lasts 3 to 8 years depending on the device
lng
As of 2025, different levonorgestrel IUDs are labeled for between 3 and 8 years, and none lasts as long as the copper IUD.
Ovulation often continues because the effect is local
lng
Most of the action is local, with thickened cervical mucus and a thin endometrium and little systemic hormone, so many users keep ovulating.
No hormone; copper causes a sterile inflammatory reaction toxic to sperm
cu
Copper ions provoke a local inflammatory response in the uterus that is toxic to sperm and ova, so fertilization rarely happens and no hormone enters the body.
Periods become heavier and more painful
cu
The device adds inflammation without suppressing the endometrium, so bleeding and cramping increase, a common reason users have it removed.
Most effective emergency contraception when placed within 5 days
cu
Inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex it prevents fertilization more reliably than any pill, and it then continues as long-term contraception.
Remains an option for a patient with current breast cancer
cu
Hormonal methods are avoided when breast cancer is current because the tumor may respond to hormones. A nonhormonal copper device carries no such risk.
